newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIAN JOB MARKET STILL SEEN WEAK DESPITE RISE.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIAN JOB MARKET STILL SEEN WEAK DESPITE RISE.

text.p: Tentative signs of some improvement in Australia's stalled labour market during July were welcomed by analysts on Thursday but they cautioned that it was just one month's set of numbers and the overall market remained weak.

With the labour market seen as the key to further rate cuts, given the role it has played in the five cuts delivered over the past year, there was something in the data for those looking for a cut and those who believed the easing cycle had come to an end. Total employment rose by 21,300 in July, close to median expectations of a 25,000 rise, official data showed.
"I think we need a few more months of strong employment growth before we can shut the book on the weak labour market story," Toronto Dominion chief economist Gavin Stacey said.
The rise did little to change the view of a subdued jobs market which has yet to fully recover from May's 40,300 fall.
Despite the jobs rise, the unemployment rate moved higher, to 8.7 percent from 8.5 percent in June.

"It just continues to show that the labour market is in a very modest, almost flat, trend, which is not surprising when you look at business surveys and how the economy is growing," Bankers Trust Australia senior economist Peter Munckton said.
The most positive news in the figures for analysts was a 52,500 rise in full-time employment, one area of the labour market that has been particularly weak over the past year.
However, despite the hefty rise, full-time employment levels are still below the level of July last year, and a total of 11,400 full-time jobs have been lost this year the data showed.

Strength in full-time employment is seen as crucial to a widespread economic recovery, as not only do they give consumers greater spending power but because they are seen as more permanent than part-time jobs they tend to have a greater impact on confidence as well.

"From a growth standpoint, full-time employment is what ultimately will drive any recovery in private consumption, and that's obviously been the missing link in the recovery to date," Toronto Dominion's Stacey said.

The ongoing weakness in the labour market, against a backdrop of low inflation, has been a key factor in the Reserve Bank's decisions to cut official interest rates on five occassions since July 31 last year.
With the data seen as doing little to change the view of a sluggish labour market, the data also had little impact of views as to whether there would be another cut in interest rates.

"If you're inclined to think there's another rate cut, you still argue one out of this and if you're inclined to think there isn't one, you can back up that up that view with the full-time employment rise giving a hint of some improvement to come," UBS Australia chief economist Stephen Roberts said.
Those looking for another cut pointed to the slow pace of jobs growth and an unemployment rate stalled above 8.5 percent.

"The unemployment rate is really stuck above 8.5 percent and we don't see that coming down in a hurry. The figures still maintain an easing bias to policy," Merrill Lynch Australia chief economist Nigel Douglas said.

When the first cut was delivered last year, the then RBA Governor, Bernie Fraser, noted that an earlier downtrend in the unemployment rate had stalled at around 8.5 percent. Since that first cut, the unemployment rate has not been below 8.5 percent.
The government has argued that as monetary policy operates with a lag of some 12-18 months, it would not be some time before there was any impact on employment.
Economists who saw the end of the easing cycle said that as it was now a year since the first cut, the impacts of the cuts on employment growth should soon start to become more apparent.
